# The Weather Line

Every morning at 5:40, Marguerite Okafor recorded the weather for a telephone number that almost no one called anymore.

The station had installed the line in 1971, when the valley's farmers wanted to know about frost before they drove out to the orchards. You dialed the number, and a voice told you the temperature, the wind, the chance of rain, and whether the pass was open. In those days the line took eleven hundred calls a morning. The phone company had to add a second trunk.

Now there were apps. There were radar maps that moved like living things, green and yellow blooms crawling across the screen. There were watches that buzzed on your wrist before the first drop fell. The line took, on average, four calls a day, and Marguerite had come to suspect that three of those were wrong numbers.

The fourth was someone else.

She knew about the fourth caller because the system logged every call: time, duration, and the last four digits of the number. Most calls lasted six seconds, long enough for someone to realize they had not reached the pharmacy. But every morning at 6:15, a number ending in 2209 called and stayed on the line for the full recording, one minute and fifty seconds, and then called back and listened again.

It had been doing this for three years.

Marguerite was the only person left at the station who knew the line existed. The station manager, a cheerful man named Dev who had come over from a marketing firm, once asked her why they were still paying for it. She told him it was mandated by the original broadcast license. This was not true. She did not know why she said it. Dev nodded and wrote something down and never asked again.

---

The recording itself took four minutes to make, even though it was less than two minutes long. She wrote a script first, in pencil, on the back of old printouts. She had inherited the job from a man named Harold Beck, who had done it for twenty-six years, and Harold had taught her that the weather line was not the same as a forecast.

"A forecast is for everybody," he told her, the week before he retired. "The line is for one person standing in a kitchen at dawn, trying to decide something."

So she did not say *precipitation*. She said *rain*. She did not say *a 60 percent chance*. She said *more likely than not, so bring the good umbrella, not the one that folds*. When the first snow came to the high pass, she said so plainly and then added that the aspens near the Lindqvist turnoff had gone gold, because they had, and because someone listening might want to know.

She wondered, sometimes, whether 2209 was a farmer. Whether 2209 was old. Whether 2209 was lonely or blind or simply a person of habit who had called the weather line with a parent as a child and had never seen a reason to stop.

She wondered whether 2209 called twice because the first time was for listening and the second was for company.

---

In February, the phone company sent a letter. The trunk line was being retired. The station could migrate the number to a digital service at a cost of four hundred dollars a month, or let it go.

Marguerite brought the letter to Dev.

"Four hundred a month," he said, "for four calls a day."

"Two of them are the same person," she said.

He looked at her for a long moment. He was not a bad man. He had a daughter who drew horses on the whiteboard in his office, and he left them up for weeks.

"I can't justify it," he said. "I'm sorry. I really am."

The line would go dead on the first of March.

---

She spent a week deciding what to do. She considered finding the number: the log had only the last four digits, but she knew someone at the phone company, and she could imagine asking. She could imagine calling. *Hello, you don't know me, I'm the weather.* She could not imagine what would come after that.

In the end, she did what Harold would have done. She wrote a script.

On the last morning, February 28th, she came in early. The studio was dark except for the green light of the board. Outside, the valley was blue with the hour before sunrise, and a thin fog lay along the river like something sleeping.

She pressed record.

"Good morning. It's thirty-one degrees in town and colder by the river, where the fog is sitting low and should burn off by nine. Wind from the northwest, gentle. No rain today, and none tomorrow. The pass is open. Chains advised above the tunnel.

"This is the last morning for this line. After today, the number won't ring through. I wanted to say that plainly, so no one wonders.

"If you've been calling every morning, and I think one of you has, I want you to know I've been glad of it. I don't know who you are. I've made up a few stories. In most of them you have a window over the sink, and you look out at the sky while you listen, to check whether I'm right.

"I'm usually right. Not always.

"There's a free weather service on the radio at 91.3, every hour on the hour. It's a computer voice, but it's accurate. And the sky is still there. It was always the real forecast. I just read it out loud.

"The aspens are bare now, but there are buds on the willows by the Lindqvist turnoff. Spring's closer than it looks.

"Bring a coat. Take care of yourself. Thank you for listening."

She stopped the recording and played it back once and did not change anything.

At 6:15, the log showed a call from 2209. One minute and fifty-eight seconds.

Then nothing. No second call.

Marguerite sat in the green dark and waited. At 6:19, the line lit again. 2209. She watched the seconds count up on the display, past the length of the message, past two minutes, three. The recording had ended; whoever it was was listening to silence now, to the faint hiss of a line about to disappear.

At four minutes and twelve seconds, the call ended.

She turned off the board. Outside, the fog was lifting off the river exactly as she'd said it would, and the first light was coming over the ridge, and somewhere in the valley, she was almost certain, a person was standing at a window, checking.
